system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-01-09 07:15:00 to 2169-01-11 17:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

Activity Status: Ambulatory - Independent.

 
Discharge Instructions:
Discharge Instructions: Please call your surgeon or return to 
the emergency department if you develop a fever greater than 
101.5, chest pain, shortness of breath, severe abdominal pain, 
pain unrelieved by your pain medication, severe nausea or 
vomiting, severe abdominal bloating, inability to eat or drink, 
foul smelling or colorful drainage from your incisions, redness 
or swelling around your incisions, or any other symptoms which 
are concerning to you.

Diet: Stay on Stage III diet until your follow up appointment. 
Do not self advance
diet, do not drink out of a straw or chew gum.

Medication Instructions:
Resume your home medications, CRUSH ALL PILLS.
You will be starting some new medications:
1.  You are being discharged on medications to treat the pain 
from your operation. These medications will make you drowsy and 
impair your ability to drive a motor vehicle or operate 
machinery safely. You MUST refrain from such activities while 
taking these medications.
2. You should begin taking a chewable complete multivitamin with 
minerals. No gummy vitamins.
3. You will be taking Zantac liquid ___ mg twice daily for one 
month. This medicine prevents gastric reflux.
4. You will be taking Actigall 300 mg twice daily for 6 months. 
This medicine prevents you from having problems with your 
gallbladder.
5. You should take a stool softener, Colace, twice daily for 
constipation as needed, or until you resume a normal bowel 
pattern.
6. You must not use NSAIDS (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory 
drugs) Examples are Ibuprofen, Motrin, Aleve, Nuprin and 
Naproxen. These agents will cause bleeding and ulcers in your 
digestive system.

Activity:
No heavy lifting of items ___ pounds for 6 weeks. You may 
resume moderate
exercise at your discretion, no abdominal exercises.

Wound Care:
You may shower, no tub baths or swimming. 
If there is clear drainage from your incisions, cover with 
clean, dry gauze. 
Your steri-strips will fall off on their own. Please remove any 
remaining strips ___ days after surgery.
Please call the doctor if you have increased pain, swelling, 
redness, or drainage from the incision sites. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ woman with morbid obesity and esophageal dysmotility,
status post gastric bypass.

SINGLE CONTRAST UPPER GI SERIES:  Scout views demonstrate no free air under
the diaphragm.  A drain is noted within the left upper quadrant.  Surgical
clips are seen along the left mid abdomen.  Due to table restrictions related
to weight, the exam was performed only in the upright position.  Water-soluble
contrast followed by thin barium was used in the study.  Contrast was noted to
pass freely through the esophagus filling the included portion of the stomach
with prompt emptying into the jejunum at the site of gastrojejunal
anastomosis.  There is no evidence of dehiscence or escape of barium into the
excluded stomach.

IMPRESSION:  Status post gastric bypass with no evidence of obstruction or
leak. Findings discussed with ___ at 11:21pm on ___.

diagnoses.long_title: Body Mass Index 40 and over, adult

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team. You’re here today for your gastric bypass surgery, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been preparing for this for a long time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see from your chart you’ve struggled with weight for years and tried programs like Weight Watchers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve lost weight before, but it always comes back. I want to be healthier for my family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Your BMI is 40, which qualifies as class III obesity, and surgery can be very effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have sleep apnea and acid reflux. I hope this helps with those too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It very likely will. Many patients see improvement in both conditions after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would be a big relief. I use CPAP every night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your progress closely. Right now, we’re going to get you prepped for surgery. Any questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m ready. Just a little nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely normal. You’re in good hands. We’ll see you after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re back in your room. The surgery went very well — laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and an endoscopy. You tolerated everything well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. I feel groggy, but okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be on a pain pump for now — Dilaudid PCA — so you can control your discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to eat soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Tomorrow we’ll start with clear liquids — that’s stage one. We’ll advance slowly to make sure there’s no leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. My pain is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We did an upper GI study this morning with contrast, and there’s no sign of a leak or blockage. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. Can I start drinking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with clear liquids — water, broth, apple juice — in small amounts. That’s stage one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I stay on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually a day or two. We’ll move you to pureed foods next, then soft solids. You’ll be on stage three by discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my regular medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume them, but you’ll need to crush all pills for now — your stomach is smaller and can’t handle whole tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Even my antidepressant and Abilify?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them — citalopram, Abilify, lorazepam, and your pantoprazole for reflux. We’ll make sure they’re crushed and mixed with soft food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re advancing your diet to stage three today — soft foods like mashed potatoes and scrambled eggs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’m hungry but trying to go slow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Small, frequent meals — about ½ cup at a time. And no straws or gum — that can cause bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know that. Why no straws?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can make you swallow air, which leads to bloating and discomfort. It’s best to avoid them for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re cleared to go home today. You’ve tolerated stage three diet, your incisions are dry, and you’re walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on the stage three diet until your follow-up. Crush all pills, take your new meds — Protonix for reflux, Actigall for your gallbladder, and Colace for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Roxicet as needed, but don’t drive or operate machinery — it can make you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have my sister help me at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Also, no heavy lifting over 10 pounds for six weeks. You can shower, but no baths or swimming yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if something goes wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us or go to the ER if you have a fever over 101.5, severe pain, vomiting, or redness around your incisions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll watch for that. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did great. Follow up with Dr. Evans in two weeks. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass due to class III morbid obesity with a BMI of 40. She also had comorbid obstructive sleep apnea, gastroesophageal reflux, polycystic ovary syndrome, and fatty liver disease. The surgery was performed successfully, and she tolerated the procedure well. Postoperatively, an upper GI study confirmed no anastomotic leak, and her diet was advanced from clear liquids to stage three over the hospital stay. Pain was controlled with oral Roxicet, and she remained ambulatory. She was discharged home with instructions to continue crushed medications, follow a stage three diet, avoid straws and heavy lifting, and monitor for signs of complications. Follow-up was scheduled in two weeks.
